title: Topic 1: everyday phrases
method: Same plan as topic-01.uz.json, with English sound-alike keywords; kept under the ElevenLabs free monthly quota.
script: [warmly] Hey there! Close your eyes for a second.
Picture this: you just walked out of the airport in Seoul. Everyone around you speaks Korean... and your heart beats a little faster.
[reassuring] Relax! Today you get nineteen magic phrases for your first day in Korea.
One rule: when I say "repeat", say it out loud. Even a whisper counts. Words you say out loud stick much better.
Part one: thank you, sorry, and congratulations.
Memory hook: "go mow, yo". Your neighbor goes and mows your lawn. What do you say? Thank you! Gomawoyo.
It's raining, and a friend hands you an umbrella:
Who helped you today? Picture them, and say it in your head: gomawoyo.
[nervous laugh] Word two. An awkward moment!
Hook: it sounds like "mean". You were a bit mean to your friend, so you say: mianhaeyo.
Now the same idea... wearing a tie. Formal and respectful.
Joesonghamnida. I apologize. For teachers, bosses and older strangers.
Hook: "Joe's song". Joe sang terribly at the office party, so he bows to his boss: joesonghamnida.
Friends get mianhaeyo. Elders get joesonghamnida.
I'm sorry for being late. Bow, and repeat!
[excited] And the happiest word of all!
Hook: "chuckle". At every party people chuckle and congratulate. Chuckle... chukha... chukhahaeyo!
Happy birthday! Repeat, with a big smile!
Quick game. I say English, you say Korean. Three seconds. Struggling to remember is exactly what makes memory stronger.
Part two: meeting people. In any Korean shop or café, the first thing you hear is:
Hook: "Oh, so you're here! Come in!" Repeat it loud, like a shop owner!
You meet someone nice. Ask their name:
Ireumi mwoyeyo? What's your name? Ireum is name, mwo is what.
Hook: you whisper your name into someone's ear... ear-room, ireum!
[surprised] And a surprise! You spot an old friend on the street.
Hook: "Oh, you ran, man! Where have you been?" Repeat, with joy!
Jal jinaeyo? Are you doing well? The answer is the same words, with the tone going down:
Yes, I'm doing well. Jal means well. Hook: "jolly". Jolly... jal!
Your friend is leaving on a trip. Say goodbye:
Sigan jal bonaeseyo. Have a good time!
There's jal again: well! And sigan means time. Hook: "she gone". Time flies, and she's gone... sigan!
Going on a trip? Have a good time! Repeat!
Game time! I'll mix in part one too.
Well done! Missed one? Fine. Getting it wrong and then hearing the answer is one of the strongest ways to learn.
Part three: reactions. These make you sound like a real Korean.
No exam tomorrow! And the reply: geuraeyo? Really?!
Hook: "great, yo?" Fun fact: with a falling tone, it means "okay".
A friend asks if a movie is good. You're... not sure.
[thoughtful] Geulsseyo. Well... hmm. Hook: "gosh, say..." and a shrug. Repeat, slowly.
Now a firm one. Your boss gives you a task:
Come by nine tomorrow. Yes, understood! Algetseumnida.
Hook: "Al gets it". Al always gets it, like a soldier. Repeat, soldier style!
Shopping! You try on a new shirt and ask your friend:
How does it look? Pretty! Eottaeyo: how is it?
Hook: "Ottawa". How is it in Ottawa? Repeat, curious!
[softly] Now the most beautiful phrase. Listen closely.
Maeume deureoyo. I like it. Maeum means heart. Word for word: it entered my heart.
Hook: maeum sounds a little like "mom". Mom's heart.
And the opposite: add one tiny word, an, meaning not. It goes right before the verb.
Maeume an deureoyo. I don't like it. The door to the heart is closed!
I don't like this color. Repeat: like it, then don't.
Game again! Three seconds, out loud.
[excited] You're amazing! One last part: requests... and trouble!
You're in a café. The magic word:
Juseyo. Please give me. Hook: "juice, yo!" Say what you want, then juseyo:
Water, please. Iced americano, please. Repeat!
Now you're in a library. People are noisy... you're losing patience.
Joyonghi hae juseyo. Please be quiet. It ends with your friend juseyo! Hook: "Jo, young ones, quiet!"
You don't look well. What's wrong? Museun irieyo.
Hook: a moose and an eel in your kitchen?! What's going on?! And il means matter. Keep it, you need it next. Repeat, worried!
[panicked] Big trouble! My wallet is gone!
Keunil nasseoyo. Keun means big, il means matter: a big matter. Hook: Ken found a giant eel in the bathtub. Big trouble! Repeat, in panic!
Now the best part: a story starring you. When I pause, say the Korean, then hear the answer.
You walk into a small café in Seoul. The owner calls out...
Your friend asks: how is it?
[surprised] Then an old friend walks in! It's been ages:
Oops, you spill coffee on her. Sorry, friend style:
The owner comes over. A formal apology:
Suddenly she turns pale. You ask what's wrong:
She panics: big trouble, no wallet!
You find it under the table. She says thanks:
She invites you to a museum tomorrow. You're not sure:
The next table asks you to be quiet:
The bill is huge. You don't like it:
Saying goodbye: have a good time!
[proud] Congratulations! You didn't just hear nineteen phrases. You used them in a story. That's real learning.
One tip: memory grows stronger while you sleep. Recall these phrases before bed tonight, and listen again tomorrow. It'll feel much easier.
Then practice with the K-TALIM flashcards. They remind you right before you forget.
See you next time! And in Korean...
